propositions.text: I dismiss the appeal brought by the Appellant, a citizen of Iran.
propositions.quote: I dismiss the appeal brought by XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a citizen of Iran.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal brought by the Appellant, an Iranian citizen.

propositions.text: The Appellant alleges he is a Gonabadi Dervish follower fearing persecution by Iran due to his faith.
propositions.quote: The Appellant alleges that he is a follower of the Gonabadi Dervish faith and fears persecution because the Iranian government is against his faith.

propositions.text: He alleges detention in 2011 and 2014 due to his faith.
propositions.quote: He alleges that he was detained due to his faith in 2011 and 2014.

propositions.text: He arrived in Canada in 2017 to visit family and filed a refugee claim after his wife told him Iranian authorities sought him.
propositions.quote: He arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2017 to visit family. He alleges that he filed a refugee claim after his wife told him on November 9, 2017 that Iranian authorities were looking for him.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant alleges he is a Gonabadi Dervish fearing persecution, was detained in 2011 and 2014, arrived in Canada in 2017, and filed a refugee claim after threats.

propositions.text: The RPD found the Appellant's allegations not credibly established on a balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found that the Appellant's allegations were not credibly established, on a balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: The RPD found inconsistencies between the Appellant's evidence and objective documents about his faith and arrests.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that key aspects of the Appellant's evidence about his faith were inconsistent with the objective documents, that his evidence about his arrests was inconsistent,

propositions.text: The RPD found the Appellant failed to present reasonably available corroborating documents.
propositions.quote: and that he had not presented corroborating documents which were reasonably available to him.

propositions.text: The RPD held the Appellant lacked subjective fear.
propositions.quote: The RPD also held that the Appellant lacked subjective fear.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Appellant's allegations not credible, with inconsistencies and lack of corroboration, and held he lacked subjective fear.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues the RPD's assessment of his religious knowledge was too narrow and microscopic.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that the RPD's assessment of the Appellant's religious knowledge was narrow and microscopic.

propositions.text: He argues he was consistent about detentions and reasonably explained subjective fear concerns.
propositions.quote: He further argues that he was consistent about his detentions and gave a reasonable explanation for subjective fear concerns.

propositions.text: He argues the RPD failed to assess his evidence under sections 96 and 97 of IRPA.
propositions.quote: Finally, he argues that the RPD failed to assess his evidence under section 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

propositions.text: He submits one piece of new evidence on appeal.
propositions.quote: He submits one piece of new evidence on appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the RPD's religious knowledge assessment was too narrow, he was consistent on detentions, RPD failed to assess under IRPA sections, and submits new evidence.

propositions.text: I find the RPD correctly concluded the Appellant had not credibly established his allegations on a balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: I find that the RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant had not credibly established his allegations, on a balance of probabilities.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD correctly concluded the Appellant did not credibly establish his allegations.

propositions.text: I confirm the RPD decision that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: I confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court confirms the RPD decision that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor in need of protection.

propositions.text: I can only accept evidence that arose after the RPD's decision, was not reasonably available then, or could not reasonably have been expected to be brought before the RPD.
propositions.quote: According to the law,1 I can only accept evidence that: (i) arose after the RPD's decision; or (ii) was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or (iii) that could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court states it can only accept evidence that arose after the RPD decision, was not reasonably available then, or could not reasonably have been expected before the RPD.

propositions.text: If evidence meets these requirements, I must decide if it is new, credible, and relevant before accepting it.
propositions.quote: If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible, and relevant before I can accept it.

paragraphs.summary: The court must decide if evidence meeting requirements is new, credible, and relevant before accepting it.

propositions.text: The Appellant submitted a new newspaper article about a Dervish follower's execution after the claim rejection.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submitted one new piece of evidence, a newspaper article about the execution of a Dervish follower.

propositions.text: The article postdates the claim rejection, meets IRPA subsection 110(4) requirements, is new, credible from Amnesty International, and relevant to the appeal.
propositions.quote: The article details events which post date the rejection of the claim. Therefore, it meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA and is new, pursuant to the case law. It comes from Amnesty International and is therefore credible. It is relevant to the appeal because it deals with the treatment of Dervishes in Iran. I therefore admit it.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant submitted a new credible Amnesty International article about a Dervish execution postdating claim rejection, which the court admits as relevant evidence.

propositions.text: The article does not meet the test for an oral hearing as it raises no credibility issues related to the Appellant.
propositions.quote: The article does not meet the test for an oral hearing as it does not raise any credibility issues related to the Appellant.

propositions.text: The Appellant did not request an oral hearing.
propositions.quote: The Appellant did not request an oral hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the article does not justify an oral hearing and notes the Appellant did not request one.

propositions.text: My role is to review all evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.
propositions.quote: My role is to look at all of the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.

propositions.text: RAD defers to RPD if RPD had a meaningful advantage assessing oral credibility; this case does not fall under that exception.
propositions.quote: There is an exception to this, where the RAD defers to the RPD if the RPD had a meaningful advantage in assessing the credibility of oral evidence. I do not find this case falls into the exception.

propositions.text: Therefore, I will decide whether the RPD's decision was correct.
propositions.quote: Therefore, I will be looking at whether the RPD's decision was correct.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains its role to review all evidence and decide if the RPD decision was correct, finding no reason to defer to RPD's oral credibility assessment.

propositions.text: I concur with the RPD that the Appellant did not establish he was a genuine Gonabadi Dervish follower.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the Appellant had not established he was a genuine follower of the Gonabadi Dervish faith. I concur with the RPD.

propositions.text: I will address issues: religious profile, detention inconsistencies, lack of corroboration, lack of subjective fear, and IRPA sections 96 and 97 evaluation.
propositions.quote: I will address the issues as follows. (a) The RPD correctly assessed the Appellant's religious profile; (b) The RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant was inconsistent about his detentions; (c) The Appellant failed to provide relevant corroborating documents; (d) The RPD correctly concluded the Appellant lacked subjective fear; and (e) The RPD did not fail to evaluate the claim under sections 96 and 97.

paragraphs.summary: The court concurs with the RPD that the Appellant failed to establish genuine faith and outlines issues to address.

propositions.text: The RPD held the Appellant failed to establish genuine Dervish practice due to inability to explain core ideology and ceremonies.
propositions.quote: The RPD held that the Appellant had not established he was a genuine Dervish practitioner because he was unable to explain the central ideology of the faith and important components of its ceremonies.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues the RPD erred by narrowly focusing and not considering his full testimony on faith.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that this was an error because the RPD failed to consider the totality of the Appellant's testimony on his faith and was too narrow and microscopic in its focus.

propositions.text: He argues his testimony was scattered, not vague as the RPD found.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that his testimony was scattered as opposed to vague, as the RPD found.

propositions.text: I concur with the RPD's assessment of the Appellant's religious knowledge and testimony.
propositions.quote: I concur with the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Appellant failed to establish genuine faith; the Appellant argues RPD erred by narrow focus and mischaracterizing testimony; the court concurs with RPD.

propositions.text: The Appellant's testimony was vague and unclear, not merely scattered but uncertain in many answers.
propositions.quote: I do not find the Appellant's testimony was scattered, in the sense that it was given at various locations but can be put together to form a coherent and credible narrative. Rather, listening to the recording in its totality, I find the testimony to be vague, in that the Appellant was uncertain and unclear in many of his answers.

propositions.text: I do not find the RPD mischaracterized the Appellant's testimony.
propositions.quote: I, therefore, do not find the RPD mischaracterized the Appellant's testimony.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appellant's testimony vague and unclear, not scattered, and that the RPD did not mischaracterize it.

propositions.text: The RPD found inconsistent testimony on three core Dervish beliefs and music's importance in ceremonies.
propositions.quote: Further, the Appellant does not challenge the RPD's finding that the Appellant gave inconsistent testimony on the three core beliefs of the Dervish faith and about the importance of music in Dervish ceremonies.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues the RPD's conclusions were too narrow and his overall testimony credible.
propositions.quote: Rather, the Appellant argues that these conclusions took too narrow of a focus, and the Appellant's testimony on the whole was credible.

propositions.text: I find no error in the RPD's findings on core beliefs inconsistencies and reject the Appellant's argument.
propositions.quote: Reviewing the record, I see no error in these findings. Rather, the Appellant argues that these conclusions took too narrow of a focus, and the Appellant's testimony on the whole was credible. I do not find this persuasive.

propositions.text: It was correct for the RPD to expect consistent testimony on core beliefs given nine years of practice since 2009.
propositions.quote: Given the Appellant's evidence that he had been a practicing Dervish since 2009, it was correct that the RPD expected the Appellant to give consistent testimony on this point.

propositions.text: The Appellant did not need exact RIR language but was expected to recall broad concepts, which he failed to do.
propositions.quote: The Appellant did not need to testify using the exact language of the Immigration and Refugee Board's (Board's) Response to Information Request (RIR), but it was not an error to expect him to recall the broad concepts contained therein, and he did not do so.

propositions.text: The RPD did not place undue weight on these issues as they are central to the faith.
propositions.quote: Moreover, the RPD did not place undue weight on these issues, because they are central to the faith.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no error in RPD's findings of inconsistent testimony on core beliefs, rejects Appellant's argument, and supports RPD's expectations given his practice since 2009.

propositions.text: The Appellant asserts the remainder of his testimony was credible and the RPD should consider all testimony as a whole.
propositions.quote: Further, the Appellant asserts that the remainder of his testimony about his faith was credible, and the RPD was obligated to consider all of the testimony as a whole.

propositions.text: I reviewed the transcript and do not agree that the testimony as a whole was credible.
propositions.quote: I have reviewed the transcript of the RPD hearing, and I do not agree. As the Appellant argues, he did give some testimony which was consistent with objective evidence on the Dervish faith. However, I do not concur with the Appellant that his testimony, looked at as a whole, was credible.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues his testimony was credible as a whole; the court disagrees after reviewing the transcript.

propositions.text: The Appellant gave inconsistent testimony about the Dervish faith's place in the larger religious structure.
propositions.quote: For example, the Appellant gave inconsistent testimony about where the Dervish faith was located within the larger religious structure.

propositions.text: He initially said Gonabadi Dervish is a way of looking at Islam and that there is one branch in the Nimatullahi Sufi Order: the Dervish Gonabadi.
propositions.quote: He was asked about whether the Gonabadi Dervish faith was a branch of a larger religion, and he stated that it is a way of looking at Islam. He was asked if the Appellant was familiar with the Nimatullahi Sufi Order, and he stated that he was. He was asked how many branches there were, and he stated there was one: the Dervish Gonabadi.

propositions.text: The RPD's documentation states Gonabadi is one of three main branches of the Nimatullahi Sufi order.
propositions.quote: The RPD put to the Appellant that this was inconsistent with the Board's documentation stating that the Gonabadi order is one of the three main branches of the Nimatullahi Sufi order.

propositions.text: The Appellant later admitted there are other branches only after RPD pointed out the inconsistency, which is not a reasonable explanation.
propositions.quote: The Appellant then stated that there are other branches. In my view, this is not a reasonable explanation, as it does not explain why the Appellant initially stated there is one branch in the Nimatullahi Sufi Order. This is not, as the Appellant argues, a clarification, as it occurred only once the RPD pointed out that the Appellant's initial answer was incorrect.

propositions.text: This inconsistency is another example of lack of credibility in the Appellant's testimony.
propositions.quote: The Appellant alleges that his testimony on the whole was credible, but I find this to be yet another example of the lack of credibility in his testimony.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appellant gave inconsistent testimony about the Dervish faith's religious structure, undermining his credibility.

propositions.text: The Appellant gave some testimony consistent with Board documentation but overall credibility concerns are significant.
propositions.quote: I acknowledge that the Appellant gave some testimony which was consistent with the Board's documentation on the Dervish faith. However, when I consider the testimony in its totality, I find that the credibility concerns discussed above constitute significant issues with important aspects of the Appellant's testimony.

propositions.text: I see no error in the RPD's decision and note it aligns with Federal Court guidance on assessing religious belief claims.
propositions.quote: Therefore, I see no error in the RPD's decision. Moreover, I note that the RPD's assessment is consistent with the Federal Court's guidance on assessing religious belief in a refugee claim.

propositions.text: Federal Court states Board can question religious knowledge expected of claimant's position but not test theological soundness or trivia.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court has stated that, while the Board is not permitted to engage in a test of religious trivia or base the conclusions on an assessment of "theological soundness", the Board can engage in religious questioning where the Board considers "whether the claimant holds a level of religious knowledge that would be expected of someone in the claimant's position."

paragraphs.summary: The court finds significant credibility issues overall, sees no error in RPD's decision, and notes Federal Court guidance on religious knowledge assessment.

propositions.text: The RPD correctly concluded the Appellant lacked expected religious knowledge for a regular Dervish practitioner since 2009.
propositions.quote: I find that the RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant did not hold a level of religious knowledge of someone who had been regularly practicing the Dervish faith since 2009, which was nine years before the RPD hearing.

propositions.text: The RPD correctly considered evidence about the Appellant's religious practices.
propositions.quote: I therefore find that the RPD correctly considered the evidence about the Appellant's religious practices.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD correctly concluded the Appellant lacked expected religious knowledge and properly considered evidence of his practices.

propositions.text: The RPD found the Appellant inconsistent about detention dates and drew a negative credibility inference.
propositions.quote: The RPD held that the Appellant was inconsistent in his evidence about when he had been detained on the basis of his faith, and it drew a negative inference as to his credibility on this basis.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues he was consistent and explained the detention inconsistencies, which are minor.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that the Appellant was consistent and provided an explanation for this issue and that the issue is minor.

propositions.text: I do not find the Appellant's argument persuasive.
propositions.quote: I do not find this argument to be persuasive.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found detention inconsistencies and negative credibility; the Appellant argues consistency and minor issue; the court rejects this argument.

propositions.text: The Appellant gave numerous different accounts of his interactions with Iranian authorities, summarized in a chart.
propositions.quote: The Appellant gave numerous different accounts of his interactions with Iranian authorities. For ease of reference, I have summarized the contradictory evidence in a chart.

paragraphs.summary: The court summarizes the appellant's contradictory accounts of interactions with Iranian authorities in a chart.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues the evidence is consistent and translator's error explains mistakes.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that this evidence is consistent and is explained by the post-hearing evidence of a translator who stated that the mistakes in the written documents were due to his own error.

propositions.text: The RPD found the explanations for inconsistencies unreasonable for several reasons (a-d).
propositions.quote: The RPD considered all of this evidence and the explanations for the inconsistencies and found them to be unreasonable for several reasons: (a) The Appellant contradicted himself in testimony as to which was the mere detention and which was the arrest as between the 2011 and 2014 incidents; (b) The Appellant failed to clearly answer why he had changed his testimony; (c) The Appellant testified that his problems started in 2014, and when asked why he did not say 2011, he said that the five-night detention did not bother him, which the RPD found not to be logical; and (d) The testimony on this point evolved, and the Appellant was evasive.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the evidence is consistent due to translator error; the RPD found the explanations unreasonable for multiple reasons.

propositions.text: The court agrees with the RPD that the appellant changed testimony and the translator's affidavit is not reasonable to explain inconsistencies.
propositions.quote: Reviewing the record, I agree with this. While I have summarized the testimony here, reviewing it, it is apparent that the Appellant is changing his testimony as the inconsistencies are put to him. If the inconsistency was truly from a translator's error, then I would expect the Appellant to have initially stated that he was apprehended twice.

propositions.text: The appellant had counsel and declared interpretation, so it was unreasonable not to list both detentions in forms.
propositions.quote: The Appellant had the assistance of Counsel in preparing his Schedule A, Schedule 12 and Basis of Claim (BOC) forms. He declared that the BOC had been interpreted to him. Accordingly, I do not find it was reasonable that he did not list both detentions in his forms.

propositions.text: The translator reviewed notes but did not provide them, which is concerning.
propositions.quote: Moreover, I find it concerning that the translator states that he reviewed his notes but did not provide them as evidence.

propositions.text: The court finds no error in the RPD's conclusion that the evidence was inconsistent.
propositions.quote: Therefore, I do not find the RPD erred in concluding that the evidence on this point was inconsistent.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with the RPD that the appellant changed testimony, had counsel, and the translator's affidavit is insufficient; thus, the evidence is inconsistent.

propositions.text: The inconsistency is significant because the claim depends on prior mistreatment as a Dervish.
propositions.quote: Finally, I do not accept the inconsistency to be minor or insignificant, as the Appellant argues. The Appellant's entire claim is based on his risk of mistreatment based on being Dervish. Whether he was previously mistreated for this reason is highly relevant to his future risk.

propositions.text: The court finds the RPD correctly concluded the appellant was inconsistent and did not establish detentions on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, I find the RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant was inconsistent about his detentions. I find that, based upon this, the Appellant has not established that these detentions occurred, on a balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: The appellant failed to provide relevant corroborating documents.
propositions.quote: The Appellant failed to provide relevant corroborating documents

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the inconsistencies significant, agrees the appellant failed to prove detentions, and notes lack of corroborating documents.

propositions.text: The RPD found the appellant failed to make efforts to obtain corroborative evidence and found his explanation unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The RPD held that the Appellant failed to make efforts to obtain reasonably available corroborative evidence... and that the Appellant's explanation... was not reasonable given the length of time and the fact that the Appellant had Counsel.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the appellant failed to obtain corroborative evidence and his explanation was unreasonable.

propositions.text: The court concurs with the RPD's finding on lack of corroboration and notes credibility concerns.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has not challenged this finding, and reviewing the record, I concur with it. While there is case law suggesting that a lack of corroborating documents alone is not reason to reject a claim, where the testimony is otherwise credible, here the RPD found credibility concerns, which I am confirming.

propositions.text: The court notes the appellant alleged lasting injury and medical attention but did not provide proof, affecting credibility.
propositions.quote: For example, the Appellant alleged he had lasting XXXX XXXX from his detention, and he had received medical attention for this but did not think to provide the documentary proof. This evidence relates to the credibility of the detention, which was in issue before the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The court concurs with the RPD that lack of corroboration and credibility concerns undermine the appellant's claim.

propositions.text: The appellant had counsel and time but failed to make reasonable efforts to obtain documents.
propositions.quote: I concur with the RPD that the Appellant had Counsel and time to obtain documents and failed to make reasonable efforts.

propositions.text: The failure to provide reasonable explanation for lack of corroboration undermines credibility and supports RPD's conclusion of lack of subjective fear.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, I concur with the RPD that the failure to provide a reasonable explanation for obtaining corroborating documents undermines the credibility of the Appellant's allegations. The RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant lacked subjective fear

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees the appellant failed to reasonably explain lack of corroboration, undermining credibility and subjective fear findings.

propositions.text: The RPD considered delays and re-availment but found these concerns not determinative due to credibility issues.
propositions.quote: The RPD considered the Appellant's delay in leaving Iran permanently, his failure to claim protection elsewhere, his re-availment to Iran and his delay in making a claim in Canada, and it found that there were concerns in this regard but found that this was not determinative based on the credibility concerns.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found delays and re-availment concerns but deemed them not determinative due to credibility issues.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues he had a reasonable explanation for delays, loving his country and wife's warning.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that he gave a reasonable explanation for these issues, specifically that he loved his country and did not plan to make a claim until his wife told him that the Sepah had come to his home and looked for him.

propositions.text: The court concurs with the RPD in rejecting the appellant's explanation.
propositions.quote: I concur with the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues a reasonable explanation for delays; the court concurs with the RPD rejecting it.

propositions.text: The appellant's explanation is unreasonable given prior arrests, injury, and extensive travel including to France.
propositions.quote: However, given that the Appellant alleged two previous arrests or detentions, one of which he alleged resulted in permanent injury, and given he had an extensive travel history including at least two trips to France which postdated these detentions, I do not find the explanation to be reasonable.

propositions.text: The court rejects the appellant's argument on this point.
propositions.quote: I therefore reject the Appellant's argument on this.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant's explanation unreasonable due to prior arrests and travel, and rejects his argument.

propositions.text: The issue of delays is not determinative; credibility concerns are determinative.
propositions.quote: Ultimately, this issue is not determinative, as I agree with the RPD that the credibility concerns discussed above are determinative.

propositions.text: The RPD did not fail to evaluate the claim under sections 96 and 97.
propositions.quote: The RPD did not fail to evaluate the claim under sections 96 and 97

paragraphs.summary: The court finds credibility concerns determinative and that the RPD properly evaluated the claim under sections 96 and 97.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues the RPD failed to assess the claim under sections 96 and 97 and must determine refugee status on un-impugned evidence.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that the RPD failed to assess the Appellant's claim under sections 96 and 97 and that, despite the credibility findings, the Member had the "responsibility of determining on all the un-impugned evidence whether the claimant is a refugee."

propositions.text: This argument does not apply in this case.
propositions.quote: This argument does not apply in this case.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the RPD failed to assess under sections 96 and 97; the court finds this argument inapplicable.

propositions.text: No un-impugned evidence exists; the RPD did not accept the appellant established Dervish status or prior arrests.
propositions.quote: There is no un-impugned evidence. The RPD did not accept that the Appellant had established he was Dervish or had been previously arrested, on a balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: The appellant's argument about persecution evidence fails because the RPD held he did not establish being a Dervish.
propositions.quote: The Appellant goes on to argue that there is ample evidence of the persecution of Dervishes in Iran, but this fails to consider that the RPD held that the Appellant had not established he was a Dervish.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no un-impugned evidence; the appellant's argument about persecution fails as he did not establish Dervish status.

propositions.text: The appellant's argument fails for these reasons.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, this argument fails.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appellant's argument for the stated reasons.

propositions.text: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD decision that the appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor in need of protection under IRPA.
propositions.quote: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD decision denying refugee status and protection.
